summary: The Gemara continues the parah adumah discussion - the verse 'l'mishmerit' excludes Tur Shimon as a valid location, amoraim dispute whether non-priest slaughter of the parah is valid, and the ish iti's impurity mechanism and immersion requirement are clarified.

display.whats: Does a non-priest invalidate the parah slaughter, and what is the legal basis for the ish iti's impurity?
display.hint: The verse 'l'mishmerit l'mei nidda' does double duty: it establishes geographic requirements (excluding Tur Shimon) and implicitly addresses personnel requirements (a kohen for slaughter). The ish iti's impurity is rabbinic but immersion is still required.
display.title: Tur Shimon Excluded, and the Ish Iti's Rabbinic Impurity

learning.ahaMoment: The term 'l'mishmerit' (for keeping/guarding) is read as restricting where parah can be performed - a geographic halakha derived from a word about storage.
learning.memoryAnchor: The word 'mishmerit' restricts both location (not Tur Shimon) and handling (a kohen for slaughter) - one word, two limiting functions.
learning.learnerQuestion: What does the verse 'l'mishmerit l'mei nidda' exclude, and why must the ish iti immerse if his impurity is only rabbinic?
learning.coreTension: The verse 'l'mishmerit l'mei nidda' must do double duty - excluding Tur Shimon geographically while the ongoing non-priest slaughter dispute and the ish iti's impurity status (biblical or merely rabbinic) remain unresolved.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara reads 'l'mishmerit' as excluding Tur Shimon from valid parah locations, and resolves the ish iti dispute (R. Yehuda: no immersion needed since impurity is rabbinic; Sages: immerse anyway) by ruling that he immerses and waits until nightfall regardless.

takeaway.text: Tur Shimon is excluded as a valid location for the parah rite by the verse 'l'mishmerit l'mei nidda'; the ish iti's impurity is rabbinic, not biblical, but the final ruling requires him to immerse and wait until nightfall regardless.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume the goat itself is impure like an ordinary impurity source, missing that its 'for Azazel' designation, not its physical state, is what causes the ish iti's impurity.

misconceptions.misconception: The ish iti becomes impure because the live goat itself carries ordinary ritual impurity, the way a corpse or other impurity-source would.
misconceptions.correction: The goat is alive and not impure in the ordinary sense; its designation 'for Azazel' gives it a special status that causes the one who carries it to become impure, a designation-based impurity rather than standard contact impurity.

quizSeeds.answer: The Sages enacted immersion even for rabbinic impurity to maintain the seriousness of the Yom Kippur rite.

sugyot.finalRuling: The ish iti must immerse and wait until nightfall; non-priest slaughter of parah is invalid according to the majority view.

glossary.en: A region east of the Jordan River, excluded as a valid location for the red heifer rite.
For keeping as waters of impurity (Num. 19:9) - a verse that restricts where the parah rite may be performed.

rashiTranslations.en: 'For keeping, for the water of impurity purification' is written; this implies that these things require safekeeping until they are sprinkled from it. To support
Rav, who said that the heifer's slaughter by a non-priest is disqualified. 'The sprinkling of its water is not valid'
performed by a woman - this is explained further on. 'And it is valid only by day' - as it is written (Numbers 19),
'he shall purify himself with it on the third day.' 'From where do we include its slaughter, the receiving of its blood,
the sprinkling of its blood, its burning, and the casting of cedar wood
hyssop, and scarlet wool' - that they too should be
valid only by day, whereas regarding the matter of a woman
being like a man, there was no need for an inclusion,
since all of these already have written in them either Elazar or
a priest. 'The sprinkling of its blood' - toward the front of
the Tent of Meeting, seven times. 'This teaches'
from 'Torah' - 'this is the statute of the Torah' (ibid.), 'Torah'
meaning one law for all its services. 'This teaches from the word 'this'' -
the text establishes what is stated here and do not add to it. After
the text both included and excluded, and did not explain
what it included and what it excluded, from now on it does not
entrust them to you except to examine within it the truth
and the straight path. 'You say: behold, we learn
all of them from the sprinkling of its water' - for the disqualification of night
is explicit regarding it. 'That they are not valid performed by a woman
the way they are valid performed by a man' - as stated further on, 'and he shall take hyssop and dip it
in water, a pure man,' etc. (ibid.). 'And this,
what is its refutation' - to Shmuel, if we say
that from the fact that it is taught that slaughter is invalid performed by a woman, it is invalid
also performed by a non-priest. 'A woman - what is the reason?' From where
does he derive that slaughter is invalid performed by a woman? Granted,
regarding the receiving of its blood and the sprinkling of its blood it is written, 'and
Elazar the priest shall take of its blood' - that is the receiving, and 'he shall sprinkle'
toward the front of the Tent of Meeting - that is its sprinkling.
The burning too, just before it, has 'priest' written,
and then 'and he shall burn the heifer before his eyes' - referring to Elazar.
And regarding the casting of the wood and hyssop, 'priest' is written. But
the slaughter - from where? 'Elazar' - and not a woman -
and you must say that 'and he shall slaughter it before him' refers to Elazar,
which is how the tanna derives it, in accordance with Rav; for if it meant that
another slaughters while Elazar watches, as Shmuel expounds,
from where would he exclude a woman? Rather,
the tanna derives it from 'Elazar,' and just as
a woman is excluded from here, we likewise exclude
a non-priest. 'The entire passage' - of the heifer, just as
its services are arranged one after another.
'Some implications exclude directly from another implication, and some implications'
stand on their own - when you examine it closely, you cannot
make the method of the passage uniform, such that
all its verses would be equal to one another; rather,
some of them have this: the implication of one verse excludes
from the implication of the verse before it - what the earlier verse disqualified,
this one validates, or what the earlier one validated,
this one disqualifies. And there are verses whose implication
stands on its own, meaning that the implication
stands in its own place and does not exclude from
its counterpart; and by their order you can understand which
excludes from its counterpart, and which
stands on its own; and now he goes on expounding the whole of it. 'To Elazar' - for he was the deputy priest. 'Granted,
according to the one who says that for future generations it is done by an ordinary priest, well and good' - since the verse did not fix for it explicitly
either a deputy or a High Priest, any priest is valid for it. 'So that they should not say two
were slaughtered' - and we hold that any labor performed with it disqualifies it, as we learned (Parah 4:4): anyone who works on the heifer from beginning to end disqualifies it

through that labor, and further on (43a) we likewise say 'and he shall slaughter it' means he should not slaughter another together with it. 'Because it says 'it'' - 'and he shall bring it out.' 'For he expounds the reason of the verse' - in Bava
